{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_015nxfE7vcpHETciPL1j4dap","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A shared build, test, sign and deploy platform. All 50 microservices move onto it and their current pipelines are retired.\n- **Type:** Infra plus software. Brownfield (assumed; see Missing inputs). Not a small build: many teams, R3 trust-boundary decisions, and it deploys to production.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness and security of the delivery path. One shared platform means one mistake reaches every service at once.\n- **Worst failure:** Someone with a pull request, a stolen CI token or a tampered template ships code to production for many services. Second worst: the platform goes down and no service can ship an emergency fix.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| CI feedback time (PR → result) | p90 ≤ 15 min | ASSUMPTION: a common developer-flow target. Confirm with engineering leads against the Phase 0 baseline | V3 |\n| Runner queue time | p95 ≤ 2 min at 2× peak concurrency | ASSUMPTION | V3 |\n| Throughput (concurrent jobs) | 2× the measured peak | BASELINE (from current CI history, Phase 0) × ASSUMPTION (2× headroom) | V3 |\n| Commit-to-prod lead time | — | UNKNOWN: no target given. Phase 0 measures the baseline; engineering leadership sets the target before Phase 4 | Phase 4 exit |\n| Platform availability (ability to deploy) | — | UNKNOWN: engineering leadership sets the deploy SLO before Phase 3. The CI vendor, registry and Argo CD run in series, so together they cap it | SLIs from Phase 2; V6 sets the floor |\n| Bad-release RTO | Back to the previous image digest in ≤ 10 min | ASSUMPTION: a GitOps revert plus sync takes minutes. Confirm against incident history | V5 |\n| Hotfix during a platform outage | ≤ 30 min via break-glass | ASSUMPTION | V6 |\n| Platform RPO / RTO | RPO 0 for pipeline definitions and environment state (they live in Git); release artifacts replicated; rebuild the platform in ≤ 4 h | ASSUMPTION | V6 |\n| Compute + storage cost | — | UNKNOWN: the platform or finance owner sets a monthly budget before wave 3. Phase 0 measures current CI spend as the baseline | V4 |\n| Artifact retention | Non-release builds 30 days; release artifacts: UNKNOWN (compliance/legal owner, needed before Phase 5) | ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | Phase 1 lifecycle policy; Phase 5 |\n| Operational complexity | Platform team runs ≤ 3 components itself (Argo CD, admission controller, Argo Rollouts); everything else is managed | ASSUMPTION: a 3–5 person platform team | Phase 3 exit |\n\n**Missing inputs.** Each is followed by what changes if the assumption is false:\n1. **Brownfield, with mixed existing pipelines** (assumed). If greenfield: Phase 0 uses the first new service, the waves become onboarding as services are created, and Phase 5 and V7 are dropped.\n2. **Deploy target is Kubernetes** (managed clusters, one cloud, existing clusters per environment). If it is mostly VMs or serverless: the deploy-model row in §3 flips to push deploys with short-lived per-service OIDC roles. Admission control becomes signature checks at deploy time. Phase order stays the same.\n3. **One Git host (GitHub or GitLab) across all 50 repos, and separate repos per service** (assumed). With a monorepo, Phase 1 adds build-graph and affected-target detection, and V3 is re-scoped.\n4. **Compliance regime** (SOC 2, SOX, PCI or none). If regulated: Phase 2 adds separation of duties and evidence for change approvals, and retention gets a REQUIREMENT. This adds organizational dependencies but does not change the order.\n5. **Service owners, criticality tiers, platform team size and budget.** Wave composition and V4 depend on these.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being | Status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Installing OIDC trust and Argo CD in the prod accounts and clusters (Phase 0) | Cloud/IAM admin access and a change approval | organizational | built | ASSUMED; request on day 1 |\n| Migration waves; retiring old pipelines | Everything that depends on the current pipelines: library and package publishing, deploy-triggered jobs, auto-created change tickets, release notes, monitoring annotations, nightly jobs | structural | specified | ASSUMED; Phase 0 inventory confirms |\n| Freezing pipeline contract v1; the wave plan | Phase 0 inventory and V1 | validation | specified | plan |\n| How approvals work | The compliance regime answer | decision | specified | UNKNOWN; ask in Phase 0 |\n| V2 sign-off | A review slot with the security lead | organizational | Phase 3 can't open to user traffic until it lands | Book in Phase 0 |\n| Any service receiving user traffic from the new path | V2 (trust boundary), V6 (break-glass) | risk/security | exposed | plan |\n| Admission enforcement on user-facing namespaces | V6 (deploys fail closed, so break-glass must be proven first) | risk/security | hardened | plan |\n| Runner fleet design | V3 | validation | specified | plan |\n| Waves 3–4; the CI vendor plan tier | V4, and procurement if larger runners or seats are needed | economic + organizational | committed | plan / ASSUMED |\n| Auto-promotion to prod | V5 | validation | exposed | plan |\n| Services that run database migrations (mostly wave 4) | The expand/contract migration step (Phase 3) | structural | exposed | ASSUMED; inventory confirms |\n| Each wave | Service owners' time, committed by their engineering managers | organizational | committed | ASSUMED |\n| Revoking old pipeline credentials | V7 | risk/security + organizational | committed | plan |\n\nAll seven dependency kinds bind somewhere above.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Deploy model: push vs pull (sync vs async) | R3: this is where the production trust boundary sits | **Pull (GitOps).** CI builds, signs and pushes an image to the registry by digest, then opens a PR that bumps the digest in an environment config repo. Argo CD in each cluster pulls and applies it. CI never holds prod cluster credentials. | Deploy targets are Kubernetes | V2 | V2 fails, or the inventory shows most targets are not Kubernetes → push deploys with short-lived OIDC roles scoped per service and environment |\n| Admission when signing or policy checks are unavailable (consistency vs availability) | R3: failing open bypasses the trust boundary, and that harm can't be undone | **Fail closed**, with an audited break-glass path | Break-glass works within the 30 min hotfix target | V2 (fail closed holds), V6 (break-glass works) | V6 fails → make admission highly available before more services are enforced. Never fail open |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: a leaked secret or personal data in logs can't be taken back | No production data and no long-lived secrets in CI. Tests use synthetic fixtures. Logs are masked and kept 30 days. Services get runtime secrets from the existing secret manager. | No service's tests need production data | V2 (its test cases include secret leaks) | A service needs prod-like test data → build a separate masked-data pipeline with its own gate |\n| Pipeline contract (how a service declares build, test and deploy) | R2: 50 repos consume it, so changing it means coordinated change across teams | Versioned reusable templates (GitHub reusable workflows or GitLab includes), one per archetype, pinned by semver tag. Each repo has a `service.yaml` with only declared parameters, plus one declared custom-step slot. Renovate opens the PRs that bump template versions. | A few archetypes cover the fleet | V1 | V1 fails → more archetypes or a wider escape hatch, and wave sizes are re-planned |\n| Artifact identity and provenance | R2: changing it later means re-signing artifacts and rewriting admission policy everywhere | Immutable OCI digests. Signed with cosign using a cloud KMS key (not keyless, so repo names stay out of public transparency logs). SLSA provenance and an SBOM (syft) attached to each image. | Admission can verify all three fast enough | Phase 1 pilot: sign and verify on every archetype | Offline or air-gapped verification needed → bundle keys and attestations with the artifact |\n| Build vs buy: CI engine | R2 | Buy: use the CI built into the existing Git host | One Git host is standard across all repos | Phase 1 pilot | Mandated on-prem or air-gapped CI → self-hosted engine, and re-plan |\n| Runner hosting | R2 | Vendor-hosted runners. Fork and PR builds run isolated with no secrets. | Hosted capacity and cost hold up | V3, V4 | V3 or V4 fails → self-hosted, autoscaled runners (Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes) for the heavy archetypes |\n| Platform shape (monolith vs services) | R2 | Assemble managed and OSS parts with thin glue. No custom platform services and no portal in v1. | Small platform team | Phase 3 exit: platform toil per week stays within team capacity | Repeated manual onboarding work swamps the team → build a self-service layer (see §10) |\n| (Brownfield) Migration strategy, coexistence, system of record, rollback | R2 | **Replatform the pipelines, not the services.** Before cutover, the new path deploys a separate internal-only deployment and Argo CD does not manage the user-facing one. At cutover, Argo CD adopts the user-facing resource and the old pipeline's deploy step is switched off but kept. Per service, a flag in the service catalog names the single path that is the source of truth. **Rollback:** pause Argo CD auto-sync for that app and switch the old step back on. | Old pipelines can be switched off without being deleted | Phase 1 pilots; V7 | A service's old pipeline can't be switched off cleanly → it migrates in wave 4, after its pipeline is refactored |\n\n**R1 defaults:** Kyverno for admission (`verifyImages`); Argo Rollouts for canaries; syft for SBOMs; build cache in the vendor's cache; notifications to the owning team's chat channel; existing linters and test runners kept per language.\n**N/A:** prompt+RAG vs fine-tune and hosted vs self-hosted model (no AI component); tenancy model (one organization; team access is handled in V2's RBAC).\n**Kept as they are (cost to change):** Git host and repo layout (months, every repo); existing clusters and environment set (weeks per environment); observability stack and secret manager (weeks, cross-team). The plan uses these and does not redesign them.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The real request:** a real commit to `main` of one low-risk, stateless service with a willing owner. The response is that exact commit running in the production cluster, answering a real HTTP request, and visible on one trace.\n- **Tiers crossed:**\n  1. Git host (protected `main`)\n  2. CI job on a hosted runner using template v0\n  3. Unit tests\n  4. Image build\n  5. Signing, SBOM and provenance\n  6. Registry push by digest, authenticated with OIDC (no static keys)\n  7. Auto-PR to the environment config repo\n  8. Argo CD syncs staging, then a manually approved sync to prod\n  9. Kyverno checks the image in **audit mode**\n  10. Prod cluster and the service pod\n  11. Telemetry\n- **Deployed:** by the pipeline itself. The platform's own pieces (Argo CD, Kyverno, OIDC roles, registry) are Terraform/Helm in a platform repo.\n- **Logged:** CI and Argo CD logs go to the central log store, tagged with commit SHA and image digest.\n- **Monitored:**\n  - CI run, deploy event and service request share one trace (OpenTelemetry exporter for CI, deploy annotations on dashboards).\n  - Alerts fire on a failed `main` build, an Argo CD sync that fails or degrades, and service health.\n- **Rolled back:** `git revert` in the environment repo, then Argo CD syncs the previous digest.\n- **Who can reach it:** the new path deploys `<svc>-next`, a separate deployment in the prod namespace. It is routed only for requests carrying an internal header from the corporate network. User traffic stays on the deployment built by the old pipeline, which remains the source of truth and the fallback. Only the platform team and the service owner can change templates and the environment repo.\n- **Alongside:**\n  - Inventory all 50 services: language, build tool, deploy target, database migrations, secrets, owner, criticality, and what depends on the old pipeline (each marked CONFIRMED or ASSUMED).\n  - Export baselines from current CI history: builds per day, peak concurrency, durations, spend.\n  - Start the organizational items in §2.\n\n**Exit check (V0):**\n- A real commit reaches prod `<svc>-next` with one trace across every tier.\n- One deploy and one rollback succeed through the pipeline.\n- A build with a deliberately failing readiness probe fires the sync-degraded alert.\n- First values are recorded as baselines: commit-to-prod time, queue time, cost per run.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Pipeline contract and artifact identity** (the change that would cause the most rework if wrong)\n  - **Unlocks:** contract v1 and the wave plan.\n  - **Depends on:** V0 and the Phase 0 inventory.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Cluster the inventory into archetypes.\n    2. Write the `service.yaml` schema and template v1 per archetype, with semver tags and Renovate bump PRs.\n    3. Fix the artifact identity scheme (digest, tags, KMS signing, SBOM, provenance) and the environment repo layout (an app-of-apps per environment).\n    4. Pilot one service per archetype (about 4–6) through staging, plus an internal-only prod `-next` deployment.\n    5. Set registry lifecycle rules (30-day non-release retention, release artifacts kept).\n    6. Run V1.\n  - **Rollback:** pilots return to template v0 or their old pipeline; no user traffic is affected.\n  - **Exit check:** V1 passes; contract v1.0 is tagged; each pilot builds with a cold cache.\n\n- **Phase 2: Trust boundary and production admission** (controls the worst failure)\n  - **Unlocks:** user traffic on the new path.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 1 and the security lead's review slot.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Scope OIDC trust per repo, branch and environment. CI's only cloud permission is registry push from protected branches.\n    2. Remove static credentials from the new path.\n    3. Add CODEOWNERS and required reviews on the templates and environment repos.\n    4. Give fork PRs no secrets.\n    5. Turn on secret scanning and push protection, and log masking.\n    6. Write Kyverno policies as code, with tests: signed by the platform key, approved registry only, digest-pinned.\n    7. Enforce them on the pilot `-next` namespaces only.\n    8. Run Kyverno with 2+ replicas and document its failure policy.\n    9. Build the break-glass procedure (time-boxed role, page on use, after-the-fact review).\n    10. Run V2, then V6.\n  - **Rollback:** admission back to audit mode per namespace. User traffic is still on the old pipelines.\n  - **Exit check:** V2 and V6 pass; deploy and break-glass audit logs reach the SIEM.\n\n- **Phase 3: Safe delivery, capacity, and wave 1** (the pilots take user traffic)\n  - **Unlocks:** waves at scale.\n  - **Depends on:** V2, V6, and the deploy SLO input.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Add Argo Rollouts canaries with automated analysis on the service's SLO metrics (steps 5% → 25% → 100%).\n    2. Add a pre-deploy database migration job (expand/contract, least-privilege database role).\n    3. Cut over the pilots (Argo CD adopts the user-facing deployment; old deploy step switched off). Promotion to prod still needs manual approval.\n    4. Enforce admission on the pilots' namespaces.\n    5. Run V5 on the pilots; when it passes, enable auto-promotion.\n    6. Run V3 as a synthetic load test.\n    7. Start metering cost per run for V4.\n    8. Publish DORA metrics dashboards.\n  - **Rollback:** per service, flip the source-of-truth flag back, pause Argo CD auto-sync, switch the old deploy step back on.\n  - **Exit check:** V5 and V3 pass; pilots deploy to users only through the new path; platform toil per week is within the complexity budget.\n\n- **Phase 4: Migration waves** (exposure grows from smallest to largest)\n  - **Unlocks:** the whole fleet on the platform.\n  - **Depends on:** V3 (before wave 2); V4 and any procurement (before wave 3).\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Wave 2: about 10 low-criticality stateless services.\n    2. Wave 3: about 20 services.\n    3. Wave 4: the remaining 14 or so, including tier-1, stateful and odd-case services.\n    4. Each wave: a generated onboarding PR, owner review, a week on the internal `-next` deployment, cutover, then admission enforced on that namespace.\n    5. Re-point what depended on the old pipelines (package publishing, change tickets, release notes) as each service moves.\n    6. A wave halts if change-failure rate or queue time goes past its baseline or its V3 bar.\n  - **Rollback:** per-service flag, as in Phase 3.\n  - **Exit check:** all 50 services deploy only through the platform; the lead-time target is set and tracked.\n\n- **Phase 5: Retire the old pipelines and enforce everywhere**\n  - **Unlocks:** a single delivery path; old credentials gone.\n  - **Depends on:** V7 per service, the retention requirement, and V6 re-run at full fleet.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Export and archive each old pipeline's config.\n    2. Revoke its prod credentials and delete its static secrets.\n    3. Enforce admission on the whole cluster (deny anything not admitted through Argo CD).\n    4. Turn on drift detection.\n    5. Rehearse rebuilding the platform from Git (V6 re-run).\n  - **Point of no return:** revoking a service's old credentials, guarded by V7. The archived config allows reconstruction, but only after new credentials are issued (days).\n  - **Exit check:** zero deploys outside Argo CD over 30 days; old credentials are reported revoked.\n\n## 6. The CI vendor, registry and Argo CD run in series, so together they cap it | SLIs from Phase 2; V6 sets the floor |\n| Bad-release RTO | Back to the previous image digest in ≤ 10 min | ASSUMPTION: a GitOps revert plus sync takes minutes. Confirm against incident history | V5 |\n| Hotfix during a platform outage | ≤ 30 min via break-glass | ASSUMPTION | V6 |\n| Platform RPO / RTO | RPO 0 for pipeline definitions and environment state (they live in Git); release artifacts replicated; rebuild the platform in ≤ 4 h | ASSUMPTION | V6 |\n| Compute + storage cost | — | UNKNOWN: the platform or finance owner sets a monthly budget before wave 3. Phase 0 measures current CI spend as the baseline | V4 |\n| Artifact retention | Non-release builds 30 days; release artifacts: UNKNOWN (compliance/legal owner, needed before Phase 5) | ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | Phase 1 lifecycle policy; Phase 5 |\n| Operational complexity | Platform team runs ≤ 3 components itself (Argo CD, admission controller, Argo Rollouts); everything else is managed | ASSUMPTION: a 3–5 person platform team | Phase 3 exit |\n\n**Missing inputs.** Each is followed by what changes if the assumption is false:\n1. **Brownfield, with mixed existing pipelines** (assumed). If greenfield: Phase 0 uses the first new service, the waves become onboarding as services are created, and Phase 5 and V7 are dropped.\n2. **Deploy target is Kubernetes** (managed clusters, one cloud, existing clusters per environment). If it is mostly VMs or serverless: the deploy-model row in §3 flips to push deploys with short-lived per-service OIDC roles. Admission control becomes signature checks at deploy time. Phase order stays the same.\n3. **One Git host (GitHub or GitLab) across all 50 repos, and separate repos per service** (assumed). With a monorepo, Phase 1 adds build-graph and affected-target detection, and V3 is re-scoped.\n4. **Compliance regime** (SOC 2, SOX, PCI or none). If regulated: Phase 2 adds separation of duties and evidence for change approvals, and retention gets a REQUIREMENT. This adds organizational dependencies but does not change the order.\n5. **Service owners, criticality tiers, platform team size and budget.** Wave composition and V4 depend on these.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being | Status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Installing OIDC trust and Argo CD in the prod accounts and clusters (Phase 0) | Cloud/IAM admin access and a change approval | organizational | built | ASSUMED; request on day 1 |\n| Migration waves; retiring old pipelines | Everything that depends on the current pipelines: library and package publishing, deploy-triggered jobs, auto-created change tickets, release notes, monitoring annotations, nightly jobs | structural | specified | ASSUMED; Phase 0 inventory confirms |\n| Freezing pipeline contract v1; the wave plan | Phase 0 inventory and V1 | validation | specified | plan |\n| How approvals work | The compliance regime answer | decision | specified | UNKNOWN; ask in Phase 0 |\n| V2 sign-off | A review slot with the security lead | organizational | Phase 3 can't open to user traffic until it lands | Book in Phase 0 |\n| Any service receiving user traffic from the new path | V2 (trust boundary), V6 (break-glass) | risk/security | exposed | plan |\n| Admission enforcement on user-facing namespaces | V6 (deploys fail closed, so break-glass must be proven first) | risk/security | hardened | plan |\n| Runner fleet design | V3 | validation | specified | plan |\n| Waves 3–4; the CI vendor plan tier | V4, and procurement if larger runners or seats are needed | economic + organizational | committed | plan / ASSUMED |\n| Auto-promotion to prod | V5 | validation | exposed | plan |\n| Services that run database migrations (mostly wave 4) | The expand/contract migration step (Phase 3) | structural | exposed | ASSUMED; inventory confirms |\n| Each wave | Service owners' time, committed by their engineering managers | organizational | committed | ASSUMED |\n| Revoking old pipeline credentials | V7 | risk/security + organizational | committed | plan |\n\nAll seven dependency kinds bind somewhere above.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Deploy model: push vs pull (sync vs async) | R3: this is where the production trust boundary sits | **Pull (GitOps).** CI builds, signs and pushes an image to the registry by digest, then opens a PR that bumps the digest in an environment config repo. Argo CD in each cluster pulls and applies it. CI never holds prod cluster credentials. | Deploy targets are Kubernetes | V2 | V2 fails, or the inventory shows most targets are not Kubernetes → push deploys with short-lived OIDC roles scoped per service and environment |\n| Admission when signing or policy checks are unavailable (consistency vs availability) | R3: failing open bypasses the trust boundary, and that harm can't be undone | **Fail closed**, with an audited break-glass path | Break-glass works within the 30 min hotfix target | V2 (fail closed holds), V6 (break-glass works) | V6 fails → make admission highly available before more services are enforced. Never fail open |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: a leaked secret or personal data in logs can't be taken back | No production data and no long-lived secrets in CI. Tests use synthetic fixtures. Logs are masked and kept 30 days. Services get runtime secrets from the existing secret manager. | No service's tests need production data | V2 (its test cases include secret leaks) | A service needs prod-like test data → build a separate masked-data pipeline with its own gate |\n| Pipeline contract (how a service declares build, test and deploy) | R2: 50 repos consume it, so changing it means coordinated change across teams | Versioned reusable templates (GitHub reusable workflows or GitLab includes), one per archetype, pinned by semver tag. Each repo has a `service.yaml` with only declared parameters, plus one declared custom-step slot. Renovate opens the PRs that bump template versions. | A few archetypes cover the fleet | V1 | V1 fails → more archetypes or a wider escape hatch, and wave sizes are re-planned |\n| Artifact identity and provenance | R2: changing it later means re-signing artifacts and rewriting admission policy everywhere | Immutable OCI digests. Signed with cosign using a cloud KMS key (not keyless, so repo names stay out of public transparency logs). SLSA provenance and an SBOM (syft) attached to each image. | Admission can verify all three fast enough | Phase 1 pilot: sign and verify on every archetype | Offline or air-gapped verification needed → bundle keys and attestations with the artifact |\n| Build vs buy: CI engine | R2 | Buy: use the CI built into the existing Git host | One Git host is standard across all repos | Phase 1 pilot | Mandated on-prem or air-gapped CI → self-hosted engine, and re-plan |\n| Runner hosting | R2 | Vendor-hosted runners. Fork and PR builds run isolated with no secrets. | Hosted capacity and cost hold up | V3, V4 | V3 or V4 fails → self-hosted, autoscaled runners (Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes) for the heavy archetypes |\n| Platform shape (monolith vs services) | R2 | Assemble managed and OSS parts with thin glue. No custom platform services and no portal in v1. | Small platform team | Phase 3 exit: platform toil per week stays within team capacity | Repeated manual onboarding work swamps the team → build a self-service layer (see §10) |\n| (Brownfield) Migration strategy, coexistence, system of record, rollback | R2 | **Replatform the pipelines, not the services.** Before cutover, the new path deploys a separate internal-only deployment and Argo CD does not manage the user-facing one. At cutover, Argo CD adopts the user-facing resource and the old pipeline's deploy step is switched off but kept. Per service, a flag in the service catalog names the single path that is the source of truth. **Rollback:** pause Argo CD auto-sync for that app and switch the old step back on. | Old pipelines can be switched off without being deleted | Phase 1 pilots; V7 | A service's old pipeline can't be switched off cleanly → it migrates in wave 4, after its pipeline is refactored |\n\n**R1 defaults:** Kyverno for admission (`verifyImages`); Argo Rollouts for canaries; syft for SBOMs; build cache in the vendor's cache; notifications to the owning team's chat channel; existing linters and test runners kept per language.\n**N/A:** prompt+RAG vs fine-tune and hosted vs self-hosted model (no AI component); tenancy model (one organization; team access is handled in V2's RBAC).\n**Kept as they are (cost to change):** Git host and repo layout (months, every repo); existing clusters and environment set (weeks per environment); observability stack and secret manager (weeks, cross-team). The plan uses these and does not redesign them.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The real request:** a real commit to `main` of one low-risk, stateless service with a willing owner. The response is that exact commit running in the production cluster, answering a real HTTP request, and visible on one trace.\n- **Tiers crossed:**\n  1. Git host (protected `main`)\n  2. CI job on a hosted runner using template v0\n  3. Unit tests\n  4. Image build\n  5. Signing, SBOM and provenance\n  6. Registry push by digest, authenticated with OIDC (no static keys)\n  7. Auto-PR to the environment config repo\n  8. Argo CD syncs staging, then a manually approved sync to prod\n  9. Kyverno checks the image in **audit mode**\n  10. Prod cluster and the service pod\n  11. Telemetry\n- **Deployed:** by the pipeline itself. The platform's own pieces (Argo CD, Kyverno, OIDC roles, registry) are Terraform/Helm in a platform repo.\n- **Logged:** CI and Argo CD logs go to the central log store, tagged with commit SHA and image digest.\n- **Monitored:**\n  - CI run, deploy event and service request share one trace (OpenTelemetry exporter for CI, deploy annotations on dashboards).\n  - Alerts fire on a failed `main` build, an Argo CD sync that fails or degrades, and service health.\n- **Rolled back:** `git revert` in the environment repo, then Argo CD syncs the previous digest.\n- **Who can reach it:** the new path deploys `<svc>-next`, a separate deployment in the prod namespace. It is routed only for requests carrying an internal header from the corporate network. User traffic stays on the deployment built by the old pipeline, which remains the source of truth and the fallback. Only the platform team and the service owner can change templates and the environment repo.\n- **Alongside:**\n  - Inventory all 50 services: language, build tool, deploy target, database migrations, secrets, owner, criticality, and what depends on the old pipeline (each marked CONFIRMED or ASSUMED).\n  - Export baselines from current CI history: builds per day, peak concurrency, durations, spend.\n  - Start the organizational items in §2.\n\n**Exit check (V0):**\n- A real commit reaches prod `<svc>-next` with one trace across every tier.\n- One deploy and one rollback succeed through the pipeline.\n- A build with a deliberately failing readiness probe fires the sync-degraded alert.\n- First values are recorded as baselines: commit-to-prod time, queue time, cost per run.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Pipeline contract and artifact identity** (the change that would cause the most rework if wrong)\n  - **Unlocks:** contract v1 and the wave plan.\n  - **Depends on:** V0 and the Phase 0 inventory.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Cluster the inventory into archetypes.\n    2. Write the `service.yaml` schema and template v1 per archetype, with semver tags and Renovate bump PRs.\n    3. Fix the artifact identity scheme (digest, tags, KMS signing, SBOM, provenance) and the environment repo layout (an app-of-apps per environment).\n    4. Pilot one service per archetype (about 4–6) through staging, plus an internal-only prod `-next` deployment.\n    5. Set registry lifecycle rules (30-day non-release retention, release artifacts kept).\n    6. Run V1.\n  - **Rollback:** pilots return to template v0 or their old pipeline; no user traffic is affected.\n  - **Exit check:** V1 passes; contract v1.0 is tagged; each pilot builds with a cold cache.\n\n- **Phase 2: Trust boundary and production admission** (controls the worst failure)\n  - **Unlocks:** user traffic on the new path.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 1 and the security lead's review slot.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Scope OIDC trust per repo, branch and environment. CI's only cloud permission is registry push from protected branches.\n    2. Remove static credentials from the new path.\n    3. Add CODEOWNERS and required reviews on the templates and environment repos.\n    4. Give fork PRs no secrets.\n    5. Turn on secret scanning and push protection, and log masking.\n    6. Write Kyverno policies as code, with tests: signed by the platform key, approved registry only, digest-pinned.\n    7. Enforce them on the pilot `-next` namespaces only.\n    8. Run Kyverno with 2+ replicas and document its failure policy.\n    9. Build the break-glass procedure (time-boxed role, page on use, after-the-fact review).\n    10. Run V2, then V6.\n  - **Rollback:** admission back to audit mode per namespace. User traffic is still on the old pipelines.\n  - **Exit check:** V2 and V6 pass; deploy and break-glass audit logs reach the SIEM.\n\n- **Phase 3: Safe delivery, capacity, and wave 1** (the pilots take user traffic)\n  - **Unlocks:** waves at scale.\n  - **Depends on:** V2, V6, and the deploy SLO input.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Add Argo Rollouts canaries with automated analysis on the service's SLO metrics (steps 5% → 25% → 100%).\n    2. Add a pre-deploy database migration job (expand/contract, least-privilege database role).\n    3. Cut over the pilots (Argo CD adopts the user-facing deployment; old deploy step switched off). Promotion to prod still needs manual approval.\n    4. Enforce admission on the pilots' namespaces.\n    5. Run V5 on the pilots; when it passes, enable auto-promotion.\n    6. Run V3 as a synthetic load test.\n    7. Start metering cost per run for V4.\n    8. Publish DORA metrics dashboards.\n  - **Rollback:** per service, flip the source-of-truth flag back, pause Argo CD auto-sync, switch the old deploy step back on.\n  - **Exit check:** V5 and V3 pass; pilots deploy to users only through the new path; platform toil per week is within the complexity budget.\n\n- **Phase 4: Migration waves** (exposure grows from smallest to largest)\n  - **Unlocks:** the whole fleet on the platform.\n  - **Depends on:** V3 (before wave 2); V4 and any procurement (before wave 3).\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Wave 2: about 10 low-criticality stateless services.\n    2. Wave 3: about 20 services.\n    3. Wave 4: the remaining 14 or so, including tier-1, stateful and odd-case services.\n    4. Each wave: a generated onboarding PR, owner review, a week on the internal `-next` deployment, cutover, then admission enforced on that namespace.\n    5. Re-point what depended on the old pipelines (package publishing, change tickets, release notes) as each service moves.\n    6. A wave halts if change-failure rate or queue time goes past its baseline or its V3 bar.\n  - **Rollback:** per-service flag, as in Phase 3.\n  - **Exit check:** all 50 services deploy only through the platform; the lead-time target is set and tracked.\n\n- **Phase 5: Retire the old pipelines and enforce everywhere**\n  - **Unlocks:** a single delivery path; old credentials gone.\n  - **Depends on:** V7 per service, the retention requirement, and V6 re-run at full fleet.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Export and archive each old pipeline's config.\n    2. Revoke its prod credentials and delete its static secrets.\n    3. Enforce admission on the whole cluster (deny anything not admitted through Argo CD).\n    4. Turn on drift detection.\n    5. Rehearse rebuilding the platform from Git (V6 re-run).\n  - **Point of no return:** revoking a service's old credentials, guarded by V7. The archived config allows reconstruction, but only after new credentials are issued (days).\n  - **Exit check:** zero deploys outside Argo CD over 30 days; old credentials are reported revoked.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | The §4 skeleton run, plus an injected readiness failure | The V0 exit check in §4 | Trace link, deploy and rollback run IDs, alert record, baseline sheet in the platform repo | Phase 1. If it fails: fix the failing tier before anything else | 0 |\n| V1 | A few archetype templates cover the fleet | Classify all 50 services from the inventory; run one pilot per archetype through staging | ≥ 40 of 50 services fit ≤ 4 archetypes using only declared parameters; the rest fit the single custom-step slot (ASSUMPTION: if more than 20% need custom steps, templates are the wrong abstraction) | Archetype matrix plus pilot run logs in the platform repo | Contract v1 freeze and the wave plan. If it fails: add archetypes or redesign the escape hatch, then re-plan wave sizes | 1 |\n| V2 | No PR, CI token or template change can get code into prod or read prod secrets; only signed, digest-pinned images from the platform are admitted | Threat-model review plus red-team cases: (a) a fork PR requests OIDC tokens; (b) a non-protected branch pushes to the release registry path; (c) an unsigned or foreign-signed image is applied to an enforced namespace; (d) a mutable tag is referenced; (e) the env repo is changed without review; (f) a secret is echoed in a log; (g) a template is changed without platform review | The security lead (named in Phase 0) signs off on the threat model, and 100% of cases (a)–(g) are blocked, each raising an alert within 5 min (ASSUMPTION) | Red-team report plus Kyverno test output, stored with the platform repo (access-restricted) | Any user traffic on the new path (Phase 3). If it fails: redesign the trust model (§3 row 1) before any wave | 2 (booked in 0) |\n| V3 | Hosted runners meet the queue and feedback budgets at peak | A 2-hour synthetic burst at 2× the BASELINE peak concurrency, using representative archetype pipelines, including cold-cache runs | Queue p95 ≤ 2 min and PR feedback p90 ≤ 15 min (ASSUMPTION, §1) | Load-test report plus runner metrics export | Runner design specified and wave 2. If it fails: self-hosted autoscaled runners for the heavy archetypes, then re-run | 3, before wave 2 |\n| V4 | Running all 50 services stays within budget | Meter cost per run by archetype during waves 1–2; project to 50 services at baseline run volume | UNKNOWN: monthly budget from the platform/finance owner, needed before wave 3 | Cost dashboard export plus projection sheet | Waves 3–4 and the vendor tier commitment. If it fails: build avoidance, caching, spot self-hosted runners | Starts in 3, required before wave 3 |\n| V5 | Canary analysis stops a bad release and rollback is fast | On each wave-1 service, ≥ 3 trials of a deliberately degraded build. Faults trigger only on synthetic probe traffic, so users are unaffected | Stopped at the first canary step in 100% of trials; back on the previous digest ≤ 10 min (ASSUMPTION) | Rollout analysis records plus trial log | Auto-promotion and wave 2. If it fails: keep manual promotion and fix the analysis metrics | 3 |\n| V6 | A hotfix can ship while platform parts are down, and the platform can be rebuilt | Game day: CI vendor, Argo CD and Kyverno each made unavailable in turn → ship a hotfix via break-glass. Rebuild the platform from Git into an empty account | Hotfix in prod ≤ 30 min, fully audited; rebuild ≤ 4 h (ASSUMPTION) | Game-day report plus break-glass audit entries | Enforced admission on user-facing namespaces (Phase 3) and Phase 5. If it fails: make admission highly available or keep old pipelines as break-glass | 2; re-run before 5 |\n| V7 | The old pipeline for service S can be retired safely | Per-service checklist: ≥ 10 prod deploys and ≥ 1 rollback through the new path over ≥ 2 weeks with no old-pipeline use; its dependents re-pointed; config archived | Service owner and platform lead (plus the change board if one is required) sign off as pass/fail; thresholds are ASSUMPTIONS | Retirement record per service in the platform repo | Revoking S's credentials. If it fails: old pipeline stays switched off as break-glass until the gap is closed | 5 |\n\n## 7. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | OIDC registry push (no static keys); `-next` reachable only via internal header; Kyverno in audit mode; template and env repos limited to platform team and owner | One trace from CI to deploy to request; central logs; alerts on `main` failure, sync degraded, service health; baselines | Platform as Terraform/Helm in Git; template v0 pinned by tag; base images pinned by digest | Old pipeline is the source of truth and the fallback; env-repo revert rehearsed |\n| 1 | KMS signing, SBOM, provenance; CODEOWNERS on templates; enforcement on pilot namespaces | Canary analysis on SLO metrics; DORA metrics; cost per run | Rollout and migration patterns live in the templates; load-test scripts versioned | Automatic rollback (V5); no hand-written pipelines | Per-service source-of-truth flag; wave halts at the thresholds in Phase 4 |\n| 5 | Old credentials revoked; cluster-wide enforcement; static secrets deleted; quarterly access review | Drift detection alerts on any deploy outside Argo CD | Platform rebuilt from Git (V6 re-run) | Quarterly break-glass and rebuild drills |\n\n## 8. AI layer\nN/A: no AI component.\n\n## 9. Methodology exceptions\nNone.\n\n## 10. Deliberately deferred\n- **Developer portal or self-service scaffolding (e.g. Backstage):** pull forward when onboarding toil goes past platform team capacity, or the fleet grows well beyond 50.\n- **Self-hosted runner fleet:** pull forward if V3 or V4 fails.\n- **Preview environment per PR:** pull forward when teams ask for it and V4 shows cost headroom.\n- **Hermetic builds and higher SLSA levels:** pull forward on a compliance or customer requirement (Missing input 4).\n- **Monorepo build-graph tooling (e.g. Bazel):** pull forward if the repo layout turns out to be a monorepo, or feedback p90 misses V3 on large repos.\n- **Multi-region or multi-cluster rollout orchestration:** pull forward when a service needs active-active deploys.\n- **Per-team cost chargeback:** pull forward when the V4 projection comes within 20% of budget.\n- **Test-data masking pipeline:** pull forward when a service's tests need prod-like data (§3 privacy row).","ttft_ms":3228,"type":"result","duration_ms":303416,"uuid":"7e943feb-704a-43d7-9194-a249cf1bc223","ttft_stream_ms":2233,"time_to_request_ms":183,"first_content_frame_ms":2234,"queued_turn_count":0,"result_index":0}
